name: Crewe Heritage Centre
text: Your train passes near Crewe Heritage Centre, on the train's {side}, a railway museum on part of the site of Crewe's original locomotive works. Queen Elizabeth II opened it in 1987, and it holds the only surviving APT-P set of the Advanced Passenger Train.

name: Chester Shot Tower
text: Your train passes near Chester Shot Tower, on the train's {side}, beside the Shropshire Union Canal. Built in 1799, it is the oldest of the three shot towers left in the UK: molten lead was poured through a sieve at the top and fell into round drops, which were cooled in water at the bottom.

name: Bonewaldesthorne's Tower and the Water Tower
text: Your train passes near Bonewaldesthorne's Tower on Chester's city walls, on the train's {side}. A spur wall joins it to the Water Tower, built between 1322 and 1325 to guard the port, when it stood in the River Dee; by the end of the 16th century the river had silted up and left it on dry land.

name: Chester Cathedral
text: Your train passes near Chester Cathedral, on the train's {side}. It was the church of the Benedictine abbey of St Werburgh, and has been the seat of the Bishop of Chester since 1541; its building spans the 10th to the early 16th century, so every main style of English medieval architecture is in it.

name: Phoenix Tower
text: Your train passes near the Phoenix Tower, on the train's {side}, at the north-east corner of Chester's city walls. Two of the city's guilds restored it in 1613 and put a carving of a phoenix, the Painters' emblem, over the door; it is also known as King Charles' Tower.

name: Bache Hall
text: Your train passes near Bache Hall, on the train's {side}. The house before it was pulled down after Parliamentary troops occupied it during the Siege of Chester, and the hall was rebuilt in the early 18th century; it has since been a golf clubhouse, a hospital building and student rooms for the University of Chester.

name: Capenhurst nuclear site
text: Your train passes near the Capenhurst nuclear site, on the train's {side}. It began as a munitions factory, and after the Second World War it was chosen to enrich uranium for Britain's nuclear weapons; since 1993 it has made only low-enriched uranium for civil use.

name: Eastham Rake station
text: Eastham Rake station, at one end of this stretch, opened on June 7th 1995 to serve the village of Eastham, on Merseyrail's Wirral Line.

name: Bromborough station
text: Bromborough station, at one end of this stretch, opened in 1841 on the Chester and Birkenhead Railway, a year after the line itself. Direct trains to Liverpool only began in 1985, when the line from Rock Ferry to Hooton was electrified.

name: Poulton Hall
text: Your train passes near Poulton Hall, on the train's {side}, home of the Lancelyn Green family and their forebears since the 12th century. The present hall was built in 1653, and its 17th-century brewhouse has a clock tower with a carillon of 32 bells.

name: Dibbinsdale
text: Your train passes near Dibbinsdale, on the train's {side}, a park and local nature reserve named after the River Dibbin. The valley is thought to have been part of the boundary, in the 10th and 11th centuries, between the Norse settlers of Wirral and Anglo-Saxon Mercia.

name: St Andrew's Church, Bebington
text: Your train passes near St Andrew's Church, Bebington, on the train's {side}. A sandstone church stood here before the Norman Conquest, and some of its stones are still in the south wall; the tower was begun in 1300 and took about 50 years to finish.

name: Lady Lever Art Gallery
text: Your train passes near the Lady Lever Art Gallery, on the train's {side}, in the garden village of Port Sunlight. The industrialist William Lever founded and built it, and it opened in 1922; its collections include British 19th-century paintings and important collections of Wedgwood.

name: New Ferry Butterfly Park
text: Your train passes New Ferry Butterfly Park, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve on the site of old railway sidings. Grassland has been made on the thin soils of the old track beds, and 26 kinds of butterfly have been recorded there.

name: Monument to the Mersey Tunnel
text: Your train passes near the Monument to the Mersey Tunnel, on the train's {side}, by the Birkenhead entrance to the Queensway road tunnel, built between 1925 and 1933. Herbert James Rowse designed it, one of a pair, as both a monument and a light for the tunnel entrance.

name: Argyle Theatre
text: Your train passes near the site of the Argyle Theatre, on the train's {side}, a music hall opened in 1868. Charlie Chaplin, Stan Laurel and Morecambe and Wise all played there early in their careers, and in 1896 its owner claimed its moving-picture show was the first in England outside London.

name: Birkenhead Priory
text: Your train passes near Birkenhead Priory, on the train's {side}, the oldest standing building on Merseyside. It was founded in about 1150 for Benedictine monks, and in 1318 Edward II gave them the right to run a ferry across the Mersey.

name: Hamilton Square
text: Your train passes Hamilton Square, on the train's {side}, a Georgian square laid out by the Edinburgh architect James Gillespie Graham. It has the most Grade I listed buildings of anywhere outside London, and was named after the family of the shipbuilder William Laird's wife.

name: Grand Entrance to Birkenhead Park
text: Your train passes near the Grand Entrance to Birkenhead Park, on the train's {side}, three arches flanked by lodges. Birkenhead Park, designed by Joseph Paxton and opened in 1847, was the first park in the world to be made from public funds.

name: HMS Bronington
text: Your train passes near HMS Bronington, on the train's {side}, one of the last wooden-hulled ships of the Royal Navy: her hull is mahogany. The future King Charles III commanded her in 1976; she later became a museum ship, but sank at Birkenhead in 2016.

name: St James' Church, Birkenhead
text: Your train passes near St James' Church, Birkenhead, on the train's {side}, standing on an island site. Building began in 1845 in the new dock area, before there was any other large building nearby, and the church stayed unfinished until 1858.

name: St Oswald's Church, Bidston
text: Your train passes near St Oswald's Church, Bidston, on the train's {side}. Its tower was built in 1520; the first church here dates back to the 13th century, and the rest of it was rebuilt in the 1850s.

name: Leasowe
text: Your train passes near Leasowe, on the train's {side}, whose name comes from the Anglo-Saxon for meadow pastures; its sand dunes are the largest on Wirral. In 1961 and 1962 the world's first passenger hovercraft service ran from Moreton Common, advertised as running between Wallasey and Rhyl.

name: Meols
text: Your train passes near Meols, on the train's {side}, named by the Vikings from the Old Norse for sand dunes. Since about 1810 a great many ancient objects have been found there, from the Iron Age, the Roman Empire, Anglo-Saxon and Viking times, and even pre-Roman Carthage.

name: Hoylake Lifeboat Station
text: Your train passes near Hoylake Lifeboat Station, on the train's {side}. A lifeboat was first stationed at Hoylake in 1803, and the RNLI took the station over in 1894; it now has a hovercraft as well as an all-weather lifeboat.

name: Hoylake Town Hall
text: Your train passes Hoylake Town Hall, on the train's {side}, built for Hoylake and West Kirby District Council and finished in 1898. It is in the Edwardian Baroque style, in red brick with terracotta, with a front of 13 bays facing Market Street.

name: Royal Liverpool Golf Club
text: Your train passes near the Royal Liverpool Golf Club, on the train's {side}, founded in 1869 on what was then a racecourse. The Open Championship has been played here 13 times, most recently in 2023.

name: Bidston Hill
text: Your train passes near Bidston Hill, on the train's {side}, heathland and woodland with old rock carvings and historic buildings, and one of the highest points on Wirral. Birkenhead Corporation bought it for the public in 1894.

name: Barnston
text: Your train passes near the village of Barnston, on the train's {side}. The Beatles played at Barnston Women's Institute on March 24th 1962, the first time Brian Epstein had them perform in suits; John Lennon regarded it as the first sell-out of their career.

name: Church of St Mary and St Helen, Neston
text: Your train passes near the Church of St Mary and St Helen, Neston, on the train's {side}. Emma, Lady Hamilton, was baptised in its 16th-century font as Emy Lyon on May 12th 1765, and fragments of Viking Age crosses have been found there.

name: Burton Point
text: Your train passes near Burton Point, on the train's {side}, an Iron Age promontory fort that once overlooked the River Dee. In the early 18th century a new channel for ships to Chester was cut on the Welsh side of the estuary, and the headland was left inland, beside reclaimed farmland.

name: St Hilary's Church, Wallasey
text: Your train passes near St Hilary's Church, Wallasey, on the train's {side}. The present church, of 1858 and 1859, is thought to be the sixth on the site, and beside it stands the separate tower of the medieval church before it.

name: St Nicholas Church, Wallasey
text: Your train passes near St Nicholas Church, Wallasey, on the train's {side}, known as the Golfers' Church because it stands near Wallasey Golf Club. The Harrison family paid for it, and it was built in 1910 and 1911.

name: Winter Gardens Theatre
text: Your train passes the site of the Winter Gardens Theatre, on the train's {side}, which held 1,400. In the 1920s plays such as Number 17 opened here before going to the West End, and Edgar Wallace's hit The Terror played here in 1927 before a long London run; the theatre was pulled down in 1991.

name: Oriel Chambers
text: Your train passes near Oriel Chambers, on the train's {side}, an office building on Water Street in Liverpool. Designed by Peter Ellis and built in 1864, it was the world's first building with a metal-framed glass curtain wall, since a defining feature of skyscrapers around the world.

name: St Paul's Church, Hooton
text: Your train passes near St Paul's Church, Hooton, on the train's {side}, built between 1858 and 1862 for the Liverpool banker R. C. Naylor. The Buildings of England calls it one of the most spectacular churches in Cheshire.

name: Rivacre Valley
text: Your train passes near Rivacre Valley, on the train's {side}, parkland and woodland along the Rivacre Brook. From 1934 it had an open-air swimming baths, with a main pool and a shallow one in a T shape, which was at its most popular from the 1950s to the 1970s.

name: National Waterways Museum
text: Your train passes near the National Waterways Museum, on the train's {side}, where the Shropshire Union Canal meets the Manchester Ship Canal. It tells the story of Britain's rivers and canals, with canal boats, painted canal ware and traditional clothing.

name: Stanlow & Thornton station
text: Stanlow & Thornton station, at one end of this stretch, stands inside the Stanlow oil refinery. As the refinery surrounds it, most of the people who use it work there.

name: Ince Manor
text: Your train passes near Ince Manor, on the train's {side}, a grange of St Werburgh's Abbey in Chester, recorded in the Domesday Book. Edward I was entertained here in 1277, and it is one of only two monastic manor buildings left in Cheshire.
